title: Why is there hardly any criticism of the absurdity of Sorry to Bother You (2018)?

commenti.body: Well. I do seem to recall some folks accusing it of being over the top, especially in the latter going where so many concepts and ideas are struggling with each other that they kinda get in the way of the film itself, but overall it was pretty sharp and funny and for most I think the vigor and anger of the presentation overcame any drawbacks about the screenplay. Yeah, it got a little jumbled up at the end. But it was a pretty invigorating ride though.

I know this seems ontological, but as you said people aren’t criticizing it because they liked it. Absurdism, in it’s early form, wasn’t just surrealism. It was a sort of surrealism offshoot grounded in existential philosophy. The idea was essentially, and this is very reductionist, but, “Everything is too terrible to bear unless we accept how absurd it all is.”

With that in mind, it’s not just horses at random. It’s the concept of workhorses as a metaphor for the proletariat worker, which is a long-standing metaphor, dating back to at least Animal Farm (though Animal Farm was decidedly pro-capitalism and Sorry to Bother You is decidedly anti-capitalism).

Yes, it takes a turn towards the more absurd, but it’s part of a long lineage of work that uses absurdity as an answer for very bleak conditions. And to a lesser extent it’s also part of a long lineage of work using horses to symbolize oppressed workers. So I think audiences that like and are familiar with political absurdism were pretty open to it by and large.

Its been a bit since I’ve seen it but I guess I didn’t really find that it ruined any of the movie for me. It already feels absurdist to me up until that point, so while I wasn’t expecting “horse human hybrids” I wasn’t really thrown off by it. 

Does it really clash against the message? People in power will do anything for more power and profits, including turning people in to monstrosities. Their design is very off putting and horrifying which I think is meant to exacerbate the disgust we already feel at the actions of the company. It’s perhaps a surface level interpretation but there’s something that can be found there that the bourgeoisie don’t view the proletariat as human.  Also something to be said that capitalism turns people away from their humanity. 

And, while I said that they are horrifying, the absurdity of it I found also pretty funny which added to my enjoyment of the film as well.
